nameStory: Fire pink gets its dramatic name from its brilliant crimson-red flowers that seem to glow like flames against the forest floor. The 'pink' part doesn't refer to the color, but to the plant family it belongs to - the pink family, which includes carnations and their relatives.
description: Fire pink is a low-growing perennial wildflower that produces some of the most eye-catching red blooms in eastern North America's woodlands. The plant forms small clumps with slender stems reaching about 1-2 feet tall, topped by star-shaped flowers so intensely red they practically glow in the dappled forest light. It's a native wildflower that blooms from late spring through summer, making it a beacon for hummingbirds and butterflies.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant scarlet-red flowers with five deeply notched petals that create a star-like shape, each bloom about an inch across with a tubular base

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, feeling slightly sticky or fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small clumps with multiple slender, upright stems reaching 1-2 feet tall, often leaning gracefully rather than standing rigidly straight

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small capsules that split open to release tiny dark seeds, developing after the showy flowers fade

habitat: Fire pink thrives in rich, well-drained woodland soils, particularly on rocky slopes and forest edges in deciduous or mixed forests. It prefers partially shaded areas with good air circulation and is often found growing among leaf litter in oak-hickory or mixed hardwood forests.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of narrow leaves, with flower buds beginning to form on lengthening stems by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with brilliant red star-shaped flowers putting on their main show, attracting hummingbirds and butterflies throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature and split open, while leaves may take on yellowish tones before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only underground roots and possibly some dried stem remnants to mark its location.

funFact: Fire pink flowers are specifically shaped to attract ruby-throated hummingbirds - the long tubular base is perfectly sized for a hummingbird's beak and tongue, while the intense red color acts like a neon sign saying 'nectar here!' in hummingbird language.
confusionNotes: With only one recorded observation in New England, fire pink is extremely rare here and unlikely to be confused with anything else due to its distinctive brilliant red star-shaped flowers - no other native wildflower in the region has quite this same intense scarlet color and petal shape.
contextualKnowledge: Fire pink is at the very northern edge of its range in New England, which explains why there's been only one recorded observation here - it's much more common in the southern Appalachians and may only survive in very protected microclimates this far north.
compareHints: Fire pink stands out dramatically from its catchfly relatives by its intense red color - most other Silene species have white, pink, or pale flowers. Wild pink (Silene caroliniana) is similar but has lighter pink flowers and grows in more open, rocky areas. White campion and bladder campion have white flowers and very different habitats, making fire pink unmistakable when you find it.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its catchfly relatives, white campion stands out for being densely fuzzy all over, while most other Silene species are smoother.
Among the catchflies and campions in New England, bladder campion is the only one with those distinctive inflated, balloon-like sepals - this feature alone separates it from all its relatives.
Among its catchfly relatives, ragged-robin is unique for its deeply divided petals - other Silene species like white campion and bladder campion have whole, uncut petals.
Among its catchfly relatives, rose campion is unmistakable due to its completely silver-woolly appearance and intense magenta flowers.
Red campion stands out from its Silene relatives by its bright pink color and preference for disturbed, rich soils.
Among its catchfly relatives, wild pink is distinguished by its extremely low, mat-forming growth habit and spring blooming time.
Among its catchfly relatives, sleepy catchfly stands out for having the smallest, least showy flowers that barely open.
Unlike its catchfly relatives that often have white or pale pink flowers, Maltese-cross blazes with intense scarlet-red blooms.
Unlike its taller relatives like white campion or bladder campion that grow as upright herbs in lower elevations, moss campion has evolved this unique cushion form specifically for alpine survival.
Among the catchflies and campions, starry campion stands out with its deeply fringed star-like petals and whorled leaf arrangement.
Among the red-flowered catchflies, royal catchfly stands out for its impressive height and late summer bloom time.
Among its catchfly relatives, night-flowering catchfly is unique for its extremely sticky, clammy texture and strict evening-flowering schedule.
Unlike white campion and bladder campion which have white flowers, sand catchfly's bright pink petals make it stand out.
Balkan catchfly is much smaller and more delicate than the common bladder campion, which has inflated balloon-like calyxes behind its flowers.
